summary:
The United Arab Emirates screens gender identity against travel documents at the point of entry, and the practice has produced documented refusals over at least a decade. In 2025 two Israeli trans women were held for hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to check whether their genitals matched the female sex recorded in their passports, mocked by staff, and denied entry with their passports confiscated.

In August 2016 the trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was denied entry and detained for five hours at Dubai International Airport after authorities declined to recognise her gender as legitimate, and her passport was confiscated. In March 2022 the Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon, runner-up in the 2014 Miss Tiffany Universe contest, was stopped at Dubai immigration, interrogated for nine hours and deported to Thailand ahead of her Expo 2020 appearance; her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under Article 409(1)(b) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law (2021), which carries a minimum of six months' imprisonment with no maximum prescribed. The same statute also reaches unmarried different-sex couples. Prosecution depends on a complaint basis: under Article 409(5) no action may be brought except on complaint by the spouse or guardian of the complainant, who may withdraw it at any time.

Article 412(2) punishes men who disguise themselves as women to enter a women-only space with imprisonment of up to one year and a fine of up to AED 10,000. It replaced a broader previous ban on clothing 'inappropriate for one's sex', narrowing but not removing exposure for gender-nonconforming presentation in sex-restricted settings.

Legal mechanisms explicitly acknowledge and penalise nonconformity with traditional gender roles, and transgender expression or unconventional appearance frequently lead to arrest, confinement or expulsion. There is no legal gender recognition in the UAE, and sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited, highly state-regulated circumstances.

Detention carries documented risks specific to gender expression. Detainees have been held in cells designated for 'effeminate' people, and involuntary medical and psychological treatments, including hormonal therapies and detention for forced psychological treatments, have occurred in connection with suspected or established same-sex sexual conduct. Reports of mistreatment in detention include beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture. Gay conversion practices are not prohibited or discouraged by any law or regulation.

Arrests for cross-dressing and gender nonconformity are on the record. In December 2013 two Brazilian trans women who called police about prejudice they had witnessed in a nightclub were themselves arrested for 'imitating women', held until March 2014, fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported. In 2005 a raid on an Abu Dhabi desert resort netted 26 young men accused of cross-dressing and preparing a 'gay wedding'; 12 were found guilty, 11 receiving five-year sentences and one receiving a year, with initial reports that some were ordered to accept hormone treatments in exchange for lighter sentences.

A Brazilian trans woman detained in the UAE since September 2022, arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test, has accused her consulate of negligence, a case illustrating the exposure of trans foreigners to prolonged custody with uncertain consular support.

No UAE law or policy provides protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. Same-sex marriage is not recognised. Officials have publicly declared that there is 'no room for homosexual and queer acts in the UAE'.
tangentialFactors:
Censorship extends to trans-specific content. The Media Regulatory Office banned Pixar's Lightyear in June 2022 for depicting a same-sex relationship and banned Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse in June 2023 over a scene showing a 'Protect Trans Lives' transgender flag. The country's sole internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues and reportedly any site containing the word 'gay' or 'sex', which constrains the information a visitor can reach from inside the country.

Commercial and cultural pressure follows the same pattern. Amazon blocked 150 search terms including 'lgbtq', 'pride' and 'closeted gay' on its UAE site in June 2023 under threat of penalties, removing listings including Roxane Gay's Bad Feminist, and the band Steps refused a Dubai show in June 2023 over a contract clause barring disclosure of their sexuality.

The legal regime has been applied to victims as well as suspects. In July 2007 in Dubai a 16-year-old French-Swiss boy was kidnapped and raped, was initially treated by police as a suspect, and fear of being charged under Article 177 drove him and his family to leave the country; he was later awarded AED 15 million (US$4 million) in civil compensation, and his family accused UAE authorities of failing to notify them that one of the rapists was HIV-positive, delaying medical attention.

Criminal liability attaches regardless of age, so minors travelling with families are not outside the exposure. A 2012 raid broke up a gay party of 30 men in Dubai, and two Indian men arrested that year for consensual sex in a public toilet received six months each plus deportation.

Comparative indices place the country low on measured LGBTI wellbeing: it ranked 85th with a score of 37 on PlanetRomeo's 2015 Gay Happiness Index, a figure now a decade old.
localsOnly:
No LGBTQI+ support or advocacy organisation operates openly anywhere in the UAE. In Dubai no formal LGBTQ organisations or nightclubs exist, and a nightclub that sponsored a special night for the LGBTQ community was shut down by the government. Social attitudes toward homosexuality and varied gender expression, together with the likelihood of state repression, prevent the establishment of such organisations or community education. LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Article 409(5) shapes who can be prosecuted. Because civil guardianship ends at age 18, no eligible complainant exists for consensual male-male conduct between adults, so federal prosecution is not possible in that configuration; for female-female relations an unmarried Muslim woman's father or male relative may qualify as guardian under the Islamic wali concept and a married woman's husband as spouse, so prosecution remains possible where such a complainant exists.

Residents have no legal route to have their gender recognised, and no non-discrimination remedy exists in law on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics.

The Arabic children's comic Majid came under investigation in 2022, with an edition withdrawn over dialogue using the Arabic word مثلي (mithli), part of a domestic censorship regime that reaches youth-facing material.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether consular authorities can secure release or fair treatment for a detained trans national is unresolved in the sources; the Brazilian detainee's allegation of consulate negligence is an accusation, not a finding, and no outcome for her case is recorded here.

No source in the inventory states how UAE border officers treat a passport whose gender marker has been changed, as distinct from one where presentation and marker diverge; the documented denials involve female markers with male sex recorded at birth and a male marker with female presentation, and the general rule applied is not published.

Enforcement frequency of Article 412(2) is not sourced: the inventory supplies the penalty text and the prior broader clothing provision, but no case counts or sentences handed down under it.

The dates of the Cairo 52 legal review and the currency of individual reported incidents are not specified beyond those given; several underlying reports date from 2005 to 2013 and may not reflect current enforcement practice.
